attribution: Author unknown; traditionally regarded as part of the Brahmanda Purana, though this placement is doubted by scholars
period: Commonly placed around the 14th–15th century CE; dates are approximate
summary: A Sanskrit retelling of the Rama story in which Rama is the supreme Self and the narrative becomes a vehicle for Advaitic and devotional teaching.
whyRead: It shows how the Ramayana was reread spiritually: the story is retold as a dialogue between Shiva and Parvati, and Rama's divinity is explicit throughout. It influenced later devotional retellings, including Tulsidas.
story: Shiva narrates the story to Parvati. The events follow Valmiki's outline, but characters repeatedly recognise Rama as the supreme reality, and several episodes pause for philosophical instruction.
questions: Can a story be read as a map of spiritual truth?
How can devotion and non-dual knowledge be combined?

keyTeachings.title: Rama as Brahman
keyTeachings.text: Rama is presented as the supreme Brahman and Sita as his power, often identified with maya, with the narrative understood as divine play.

keyTeachings.title: Devotion leading to knowledge
keyTeachings.text: The text joins bhakti to an Advaitic view: devotion to Rama purifies the mind and culminates in knowledge of the one Self.

keyTeachings.title: Teaching sections
keyTeachings.text: Several passages are sustained teachings, including one in the Uttara Kanda commonly called the Rama Gita, in which Rama instructs Lakshmana in non-dual knowledge.
